technique.how: Patient sits upright on the bed; turn the head 45 degrees toward the test ear, then briskly lie them back so the head hangs about 20 degrees below horizontal (over the bed end or a pillow under the shoulders). Keep eyes open and watch for 30-60 s for latency, nystagmus direction and duration; sit up and repeat on the other side.
technique.prerequisites: Best applied to episodic, brief, positionally triggered vertigo with no spontaneous nystagmus; explain the vertigo may be provoked. Neck must tolerate extension and rotation.
technique.contraindications: Relative: cervical spine instability or severe cervical disease, recent neck surgery, vertebrobasilar insufficiency, carotid stenosis; use the side-lying test as an alternative.

interpretation.positive_finding: After a latency of a few seconds, a burst of torsional up-beating nystagmus with vertigo lasting under 60 s that fatigues on repetition indicates posterior-canal BPPV of the tested (down) ear; the AAO-HNS guideline diagnoses BPPV on this finding alone.
interpretation.negative_finding: A negative maneuver reduces but does not exclude BPPV (single-study LR- about 0.28); if the history is typical, repeat or perform the supine roll test for horizontal-canal BPPV.
interpretation.pitfalls: Downbeat, purely vertical or persistent (non-fatiguing) positional nystagmus without latency suggests a central cause, not BPPV; canalith repositioning should not be done reflexively. Sensitivity falls if the patient has already been treated, closes their eyes, or the head hang is inadequate.
interpretation.changes_what: Positive with typical nystagmus: diagnose posterior-canal BPPV and perform Epley; no imaging. Atypical (downbeat/persistent) nystagmus: evaluate for central positional vertigo.

estimates.population: Single primary study comparing Dix-Hallpike and side-lying tests in patients with positional vertigo (critically appraised topic)
estimates.reference_standard: Clinical diagnosis of BPPV (study methodology rated very weak by the appraisers)
estimates.quote: For the Dix-Hallpike test, the estimated sensitivity was 79% [95% confidence interval (CI) 65-94], specificity was 75% (33-100)

estimates.target_condition: BPPV (all canals) among outpatients with dizziness
estimates.population: 100 consecutive outpatients with dizziness or imbalance, 13 with BPPV
estimates.reference_standard: Concordant diagnosis by three blinded investigators reviewing a structured history (no imaging or vestibular-lab standard)
estimates.quote: positional nystagmus (sensitivity [SE] 90%, SP 63%), and the Dix-Hallpike test (SE 82%, SP 71%).

sources.citation: Halker RB, Barrs DM, Wellik KE, Wingerchuk DM, Demaerschalk BM. Establishing a diagnosis of benign paroxysmal positional vertigo through the Dix-Hallpike and side-lying maneuvers: a critically appraised topic. Neurologist. 2008;14(3):201-204.
Lopez-Escamez JA, et al. [Diagnosis of common causes of vertigo using a structured clinical history]. Acta Otorrinolaringol Esp. 2000;51(1):25-30.
Bhattacharyya N, Gubbels SP, Schwartz SR, et al. Clinical Practice Guideline: Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (Update). Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2017;156(3_suppl):S1-S47.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not use to evaluate continuous vertigo with spontaneous nystagmus (acute vestibular syndrome) - a positional test cannot rule out stroke there. Avoid in unstable cervical spine.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Positional nystagmus that is downbeat, purely vertical, non-fatiguing, without latency, or accompanied by other neurologic signs warrants MRI for central positional vertigo (posterior fossa lesion).
safety_scope.interobserver_note: No reliability data identified; the only accuracy study was rated methodologically very weak (Halker 2008). The Dix-Hallpike is itself the reference standard for posterior-canal BPPV in guidelines, so independent accuracy estimates are inherently limited.

extraction_notes: The Dix-Hallpike is the reference standard for posterior-canal BPPV (AAO-HNS 2017, strong recommendation), so quantified accuracy exists only against weak clinical reference standards. Estimate 1 is from the Halker 2008 critically appraised topic abstract (numbers derived by the CAT from a single primary study whose PMID I could not confirm, so the CAT is cited); the CAT is classed as meta_analysis for lack of a better 'kind'. Estimate 2 is a Spanish-language primary study (Lopez-Escamez 2000, abstract) whose reference standard is a blinded structured-history consensus, so it is weak; LRs computed from reported sens/spec. Froehling 1994 RCE anchor has no accessible abstract or text and was not cited. Estimates kept separate; not averaged.
